newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: PRESS DIGEST - Ireland - July 18.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Ireland - July 18.

text.p: Following are the highlights of the Irish press on Friday:

- A former auditor of Charles Haughey's Dublin electoral constituency - expelled after he became suspicious of the Fianna Fail leader's financial arrangements - is to tell an inquiry that local dealings contributed to the party's cash crisis in the early 1980s.
- The Irish and British governments will today try to rescue the Northern Ireland talks process.
- Health minister Brian Cowen was last night accused of misleading parliament in the controversy over drug trails in orphanages.

- Irish employer's organisation IBEC has warned that electricity prices for industrial users could rise rather than fall if proposals by the Department of Public Enterprise for the deregulation of the electricity market are implemented.
- British prime minister Tony Blair will meet David Trimble again on Monday in a determined attempt to rescue the Stormont talks process.
- A national transport strike may begin next Tuesday if Bus Eireann presses ahead with plans to introduce 20 new minibuses on its suburban routes in Cork, Limerick, Waterford and Galway.
- Patients have more than a one-in-10 chance of picking up infections in an Irish hospital, according to a report in the Irish Medical Journal.
- Fianna Fail has begun an investigation into the disbursement of the leader's allowance by Charles Haughey when he was leader of the opposition.
- A change in value-added-tax regulations will give a significant boost to the finances of about 9,000 small and medium-sized firms.
- A decision on the future ownership of TSB Bank can be expected over the coming months.
- Beef baron Larry Goodman last night insisted he made no personal payments to Charles Haughey.

- The Electricity Supply Board last night called for major changes to the government's plans to deregulate the electricity market after a report warned that they would lead to price hikes and power cuts.
- A constitutional referendum will have to be held to approve the new EU treaty agreed at Amsterdam last month, the Attorney General has confirmed.
